entities.name: Adolf III of the Marck
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adolf III of the Mark (c. 1256–1296) was Archbishop of Cologne from 1261 to 1296, one of the longest and most consequential archiepiscopates in the medieval Rhineland. The Archbishops of Cologne were Prince-Electors of the Holy Roman Empire, one of the seven electors who chose the emperor, giving their see exceptional political weight. Adolf III's decades-long tenure came at a critical moment in the Empire's history — the interregnum and recovery period following the Hohenstaufen dynasty's extinction.

Adolf III's archiepiscopate coincided with the election of Rudolf I of Habsburg in 1273, which ended the Great Interregnum and established the Habsburg dynasty's dominance in imperial politics. The Archbishop of Cologne's electoral role made Adolf III a pivotal figure in this transition. His management of Cologne's relationships with the increasingly assertive city commune, the nobility of the lower Rhine, and the imperial court defined the late thirteenth-century political landscape of the Rhineland.

Cologne in the thirteenth century was one of Europe's largest and wealthiest cities, the construction of its famous Gothic cathedral having begun in 1248. Adolf III's archiepiscopate oversaw the continuation of the cathedral's construction and the city's development as a major centre of trade, culture, and religious life. His long tenure shaped the archdiocese's institutional development during one of the medieval period's most dynamic phases.
